pharm: A high-potency synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid for cutaneous use that binds glucocorticoid receptors in skin to exert anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive actions, suppressing local inflammatory mediator production and immune-cell activity in corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses.
quick: Apply a thin film to affected skin 1-3 times daily (ointment usually 1-3x, cream 2-4x), per labeling
Use only if clearly needed; limit amount, area, and duration
Topical; do not apply to the breast before nursing; avoid extensive use
Local skin atrophy/striae; HPA-axis suppression with large area, occlusion, or prolonged use
summary: Diflorasone diacetate is a high-potency topical corticosteroid (available as 0.05% cream and ointment) used for the relief of inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and other eczematous conditions. It reduces inflammation, itching, and redness by acting on glucocorticoid receptors in the skin. Because it is potent, it carries the topical corticosteroid risks of local skin thinning (atrophy), striae, telangiectasia, folliculitis, and - when applied to large surface areas, under occlusion, on broken/thin skin, or for prolonged periods (especially in children) - systemic absorption sufficient to cause reversible HPA-axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and glucosuria. It is for external use only, should not be used on the face/axillae/groin unless directed, and should be used for the shortest period at the lowest effective amount.
indications: Relief of the inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses (e.g. psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, contact/eczematous dermatitis)

dosage.n: Use the lowest frequency that controls symptoms; occlusion may increase potency and absorption

dosage.d: Apply a thin film to the affected area 2-4 times daily depending on severity
dosage.n: Reduce frequency as the condition improves

admin: Apply a thin film to the affected skin and rub in gently; for external use only
Do not apply to the face, groin, or axillae unless specifically directed (high potency)
Avoid occlusive dressings unless prescribed - occlusion increases potency and systemic absorption

Use for the shortest duration and smallest area needed; reassess if no improvement in 2 weeks
Avoid contact with the eyes; wash hands after application
moa: Diflorasone diacetate is a potent synthetic corticosteroid. After binding intracellular glucocorticoid receptors, the complex modulates gene transcription to induce anti-inflammatory proteins (e.g. lipocortin/annexin-1) and suppress pro-inflammatory mediators, inhibiting phospholipase A2 and thereby reducing prostaglandin and leukotriene formation. This produces local anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, immunosuppressive, and vasoconstrictive effects in the skin. The fluorinated, diacetate-esterified structure increases potency and skin penetration relative to lower-potency steroids.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to diflorasone or any component of the preparation

Use over large body surface areas or under occlusion
Use on infected, ulcerated, or atrophic skin

Signs of HPA-axis suppression with extensive/prolonged/occlusive use
Growth in children with prolonged use

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; corticosteroids are teratogenic in animals when applied topically in significant amounts. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed, on the smallest area, for the shortest time, and avoid extensive use or occlusion.
lact: Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in human milk; it is not known whether topical application results in sufficient systemic absorption to be detectable in breast milk. Use cautiously while nursing, do not apply to the breast/nipple before feeding, and avoid extensive or prolonged use.
renal: No dose adjustment is required for renal impairment with topical use; systemic absorption is normally low when used as directed.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment with topical use; systemic absorption is normally low when used as directed.

interactions.alcohol: No relevant interaction with topical use.
interactions.diagnostics: Significant systemic absorption (large area, occlusion, prolonged use) can suppress the HPA axis - assess with cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation testing, morning cortisol, and urinary free cortisol if suspected; can cause hyperglycemia and glucosuria.

HPA-axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, glucosuria (from systemic absorption)
rare: Growth retardation in children with extensive prolonged use
emergency: Signs of systemic corticosteroid toxicity (Cushingoid features, adrenal suppression) with heavy/prolonged use

counsel: Apply a thin layer to the affected skin only as directed - more is not better and increases side effects
Use it for as short a time as possible; do not use it on the face, underarms, or groin unless your doctor says so
Do not bandage or wrap the treated area tightly unless told to - this makes the steroid stronger and increases absorption
Do not use it on broken or infected skin without your doctor's advice
Tell your doctor if the skin thins, develops stretch marks, or if the rash does not improve in about 2 weeks
Keep it away from the eyes and wash your hands after applying (unless treating the hands)
pk: Anti-inflammatory effect over hours to days of regular use
Local effect; systemic absorption varies with skin integrity, area, and occlusion
Once absorbed, handled like systemic corticosteroids; metabolized hepatically, excreted renally
Dosed 1-4 times daily depending on formulation and severity
Store at controlled room temperature; avoid freezing
pearls: High-potency topical steroid - effective for thick/resistant plaques but greater risk of atrophy and systemic absorption
Avoid face, axillae, and groin (thin/occluded skin) and avoid occlusive dressings unless prescribed
Large surface area, occlusion, broken skin, or prolonged use - and pediatric use - raise the risk of reversible HPA-axis suppression and Cushingoid effects
Use the smallest amount over the smallest area for the shortest time; reassess at 2 weeks
Treat concurrent skin infection; steroids can mask or worsen it
Children have a higher skin-surface-to-mass ratio and are more susceptible to systemic effects and growth suppression
missed: If you miss an application, apply it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one, in which case skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed application.
overdose: Topically applied diflorasone can be absorbed in amounts sufficient to produce systemic effects if used excessively (large area, occlusion, prolonged duration), causing reversible HPA-axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and glucosuria. There is no acute antidote; management is to reduce frequency, discontinue, or substitute a less potent steroid and treat systemic effects. Recovery of HPA-axis function is generally prompt on withdrawal, but gradual tapering may be needed after prolonged use.
